title: Race Conditions & Critical Sections
summary: What a race condition actually is, why plain-looking code like `i++` isn't atomic, and the formal critical-section problem it motivates.

slides.markdown:
A **race condition** is a bug where the correctness of a program depends on the timing or interleaving of concurrent operations. Run the same program twice with the same input and you can get two different answers — not because the logic is wrong in isolation, but because two threads stepped on each other's toes.

This is the single most-tested concurrency concept in interviews because almost every other topic in this group — mutexes, semaphores, monitors — exists purely to prevent it. Get this one solid and the rest of the group reads as "here's tool #N for solving the same underlying problem."

slides.sectionTitle: What is a race condition? A concrete counter example
slides.markdown:
Picture a shared variable `counter = 0` and two threads that each run `counter = counter + 1` exactly once. You'd expect `counter == 2` afterward. Sometimes you get 1 instead.

What happened: both threads read `counter` as `0` before either had written back its result, so both computed `0 + 1 = 1` and both wrote `1`. One increment was silently lost. Nothing crashed, no error was thrown — the program just produced a wrong answer, and it did so **only on some runs**, which is what makes races so nasty to catch.

The defining trait of a race condition: the outcome depends on which thread's instructions happen to interleave with the other's, not on the logic you wrote.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: two threads incrementing a shared counter — the wrong answer
Why "counter++" isn't atomic — the three hidden steps
slides.markdown:
`counter++` looks like one operation but the CPU executes it as three separate steps:

1. **Load** `counter` from memory into a register.
2. **Add** 1 to the register.
3. **Store** the register back to memory.

A thread can be preempted — or simply run on a different core in parallel — between any of these steps. If thread A loads `counter` (say, 41) and is interrupted before storing, thread B can load the same `41`, increment it to 42, and store it. Thread A then resumes, adds 1 to its stale copy (41), and stores 42 — clobbering thread B's update. Two increments happened; the value only moved by one.

The general rule: **any read-modify-write on shared data is a race unless something makes it atomic.** This is exactly the gap mutexes (next topic) exist to close.

A **critical section** is the piece of code that touches shared data — in the example, the three steps of `counter++`. The **critical section problem** is: design a protocol so that when one thread is executing its critical section, no other thread executing the same critical section can run concurrently.

Formally, each thread's code is split into four parts: an **entry section** (asks for permission to enter), the **critical section** itself, an **exit section** (releases permission), and the **remainder section** (everything else, which can safely run concurrently). Every synchronization primitive in this group — locks, semaphores, monitors — is really just a different implementation of the entry/exit sections.

Every thread that wants the shared resource cycles through these four sections. The whole discipline of mutual exclusion is about making sure at most one thread is ever inside the boxed "Critical section" at a time, while everything else can proceed freely.

slides.sectionTitle: The three requirements: mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting
slides.markdown:
Any correct solution to the critical section problem must satisfy three properties:

- **Mutual exclusion** — at most one thread is in its critical section at any time. This is the headline property, but it's not sufficient on its own.
- **Progress** — if no thread is in its critical section and some threads want in, the decision of who goes next can't be postponed forever by threads that aren't even trying to enter. The system can't deadlock or get stuck deliberating.
- **Bounded waiting** — there's a limit on how many times other threads can enter their critical section after a thread has requested entry and before that request is granted. This rules out starvation, where one unlucky thread waits forever while others repeatedly cut in line.

Interviewers use this list to check whether you think of "just add a lock" as a full solution or understand that a lock which starves one thread indefinitely still fails the problem.

slides.sectionTitle: Data race vs race condition — are they the same thing?
slides.markdown:
The terms get used interchangeably but they're not identical.

| | Data race | Race condition |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Two threads access the same memory concurrently, at least one is a write, with no synchronization | Program *behavior* depends on the timing/order of concurrent events |
| Level | A specific, mechanical condition on memory accesses | A broader correctness bug, can exist without a data race |
| Example | Two threads write `counter` with no lock, undefined by the language spec | A check-then-act bug (`if (file exists) then delete it`) racing against another process, even if each access is individually "atomic" |
| Detectable by tooling | Yes — ThreadSanitizer flags data races directly | Not always — some race conditions are pure logic bugs, not memory-model violations |

Every data race is a race condition, but not every race condition is a data race — a TOCTOU (time-of-check to time-of-use) bug can be a race condition built entirely out of individually well-defined, non-racing operations.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: races that only show up under load/interleaving
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I ran the test suite 50 times and it passed every time, so there's no race."

**Why it's wrong:** a race only manifests when the specific unlucky interleaving actually happens, and on a lightly loaded dev machine with few cores, the window where two threads' instructions overlap can be vanishingly small. The same code can pass thousands of local runs and then fail in production under real concurrency — more cores, more load, different scheduler behavior, a slower disk that widens the timing window.

**Correct model:** the absence of an observed failure is not proof of absence of a race. Treat any unsynchronized read-modify-write on shared state as a bug regardless of how many times it "passed," and reach for tooling (next slide) rather than trusting repeated manual runs.

slides.sectionTitle: Finding races in practice: ThreadSanitizer and the limits of testing
slides.markdown:
Because races are timing-dependent, staring at logs after the fact rarely finds them. Production teams reach for **dynamic race detectors** like Google's **ThreadSanitizer (TSan)** or Valgrind's **Helgrind**: they instrument every memory access and lock operation at runtime and flag any pair of accesses to the same location, from different threads, without a happens-before relationship — catching the race even on a run where it didn't actually corrupt data.

The trade-off is real: TSan typically slows execution **5–15x** and increases memory use several-fold, so it runs in CI or a dedicated race-detection build, not production traffic. It also only sees interleavings that actually occur during the instrumented run — it proves "a race exists" but a clean TSan run doesn't prove "no race exists," since a rare code path might never execute during testing.

The staff-level takeaway: prefer **designing races out** (locks, atomics, immutable data) over relying on detection tools to catch them after the fact — treat TSan as a safety net, not the primary defense.
